Penn Law professor’s lawsuit is free speech case, not employment discrimination, 3rd Circuit notes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (201 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abajournal

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006.
  • In a recent development, the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S.
  • The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial concerns was more of a First Amendment concern, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006. (Photo by Jeffrey M. Vinocur, CC-BY-SA-3.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

In a recent development, the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Philadelphia stated Tuesday.

The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial concerns was more of a First Amendment concern, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.

In her brief, Wax, a white Jewish woman, stated that Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act prohibit discrimination “on the ground of race” and “on the basis of race,” respectively, differing them from Title VII.

She argued that the the University of Pennsylvania had an alleged double standard, allowing faculty and students to participate in what she called antisemitic demonstrations against Israel without consequences but punishing her for her commentary on race.

Tech Report: 8 nonfiction books that delve into the darkest parts of sports

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1427 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’d given up smoking and the weight I was steadily gaining was regularly making me cry.
  • In reality, it took me thirteen years and two nervous breakdowns before I finally ran a mile in 7:57, not long after I ran off (not literally) with a vicar.
  • Here are eight books that each reveal a particularly dark but also compelling vision of hot sporting hell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I took up running in 2010. I’d given up smoking and the weight I was steadily gaining was regularly making me cry. My partner at the time had been a serious competitive runner and believed I’d be able to just knock out an eight-minute mile.

In reality, it took me thirteen years and two nervous breakdowns before I finally ran a mile in 7:57, not long after I ran off (not literally) with a vicar. Somewhere in the middle of all that, I’d managed to reach number six in the UK for over-forties women’s tennis. It has gradually dawned on me that sporting success isn’t the healthy, glossy, happybodymaxx endeavour that shiny people on Instagram would have us all believe.

Here are eight books that each reveal a particularly dark but also compelling vision of hot sporting hell.

Andre Agassi, Open: An Autobiography.

Sources indicate that I read Open when I was on the verge of my own tennis-related nervous breakdown (alas not involving crystal meth like Agassi’s), during a heatwave in Nottingham, in a hotel room full of little flies that I’d become convinced were going to bite me and cause such a severe allergic reaction that I would die. The prologue is one of the best pieces of writing I’ve ever encountered: the extraordinary violence of a five-set tennis match, ending with the wounded competitors lying side by side, holding hands.

It has been revealed that then there’s Agassi’s father’s $10,000 bet (later reduced to $500) that his nine-year-old son could beat Jim Brown, the famous American Football player. The fact that the book was ghostwritten (by the wonderful J. R. Moehringer) gives it an additional layer of weirdness and gothic edge for me.

Rafael Nadal (with John Carlin), Rafa.

This is basically an OCD-fest (although officially Nadal does not have this condition) about Rafa being bullied to sporting success by his Uncle Toni. There’s a chilling story about Toni refusing to let seven-year-old Rafa have a replacement bottle of water to teach him a lesson about losing the first one (you don’t need a psychotherapist to make the link with the water bottle shenanigans on court), and another about telling him he must never make himself the center of attention, even when he was the best tennis player in the world.

According to recent reports, even as an adult, Nadal describes extraordinary anxieties, including the belief that if he makes a small mistake, his mother might die. The contrast between the superhuman control Nadal displays on the tennis court and the terrifying lack of control he feels everywhere else is what makes this such a disturbing and compelling memoir.

Serena Williams (with Daniel Paisner), My Life: Queen of the Court.

Industry observers note that there’s a brilliant scene in the incredible Teddy Perkins episode of Atlanta where Teddy, played by Donald Glover, does a roll-call of famous fathers who have abused their children towards greatness. He mentions Joe Jackson, Tiger Woods’s father and Richard Williams.

Like Andre Agassi’s father, Richard Williams was seemingly determined to create a tennis champion, trying the sport with his older daughters before it finally stuck with his youngest two, Venus and Serena. He would take them to the local tennis courts in Compton with shopping trolleys full of tennis balls. Initially, Venus was the more successful and Serena was determined to beat her own sister so she did not simply become a footnote in Venus’s story.

Leanne Shapton, Swimming Studies.

Industry observers note that swimming Studies was actually the book that set me off on my disastrous tennis adventure. It was a single line in it, something about how Leanne Shapton, recovered from her dark sporting childhood, was still placing in “age-group” events. It was those two words, age-group, that made me think perhaps I could resurrect my childhood tennis dreams.

When I read Swimming Studies, I was myself trying to swim seriously, but ended up with breaststroker’s knee—which is odd, as Shapton suffered exactly the same thing. I felt a little like the book was haunting me, and that I was literally absorbing its ailments quasi-gothically.

Brad Gilbert (with Steve Jamison), Winning Ugly.

This was basically my bible during the year I played competitive tennis. Actually, that’s wrong. The Inner Game of Tennis was my bible. This was my grimoire. This may be one of the most fun dark books ever written.

Basically, Brad Gilbert tells you how you can win at tennis (and maybe even life too)—even if you are shit. You do things like turn up early and have a hit on the court with a local coach (impossible when I tried it), then shower, change and arrive late for the match and suggest starting with no warm up. Gilbert has lots of handy hints for ways to deliberately psych out your opponents with chat specifically designed to derail them.

Adharanand Finn, The Way of the Runner.

I really loved Finn’s previous book, Running with the Kenyans, which begins with a stirring account of him unexpectedly winning a 5K fun run. After that he goes to Kenya, meets some Big Characters who introduce themselves with their marathon PBs, and becomes himself a more excellent runner. It’s uplifting and inspiring.

But this book about Japanese running methods is far darker. Finn begins this one battling injury and exhaustion and then encounters the weird, workaholic training methods of the Japanese, including running with exaggeratedly short strides and accelerated cadence. There was something bleakly joyless about this book compared with the first one, but I still hoovered it up.

Christopher McDougall, Born to Run.

It has been revealed that reading Born to Run isn’t like reading a normal book—it’s an era of your life. My heart skips and I get goosebumps just thinking about it. The ecstatic descriptions of people for whom running is both a way of life and a form of transport, and the theories about primal living, squatting and running barefoot, would go on to underpin my philosophy of sport and life for years to come (and still do).

After reading this book I became a primal forefoot runner. My friend Vybarr Cregan-Reid, author of Footnotes: How Running Makes Us Human, went totally barefoot, despite various broken-glass incidents in British parks. I will never forget the wonderfully compelling romance of Jenn Shelton and Billy “Bonehead” Barnett, and how they would eat pizza and drink Mountain Dew in the middle of their ultras, like running was something even Lana Del Rey could do.

Oh, how I loved this dark and crazy book that made running seem like part religion and part disco-party where everyone successfully hides their pain.

In a recent development, W. Timothy Gallwey, The Inner Game of Tennis.

Sources indicate that the Inner Game of Tennis changed my entire life and philosophy, and there’s nothing darker than that. I found myself using it as a way of understanding EVERYTHING. The concept is that you have two selves. Self 1 and Self 2. Self 2 will quietly do things if you just leave it alone, but Self 1 is constantly judging. During my disastrous tennis adventure, I could never really get rid of Self 1 and its constant voicings of my coming glory, imminent failure, place in the rankings, what I’d tell my coach, etc.

In a recent development, one of the tricks Gallwey recommends is reading the writing on the tennis ball as it comes towards you. I’ve encountered this kind of method in other places too, like reciting your own phone number backwards during a panic attack.

Another dark sports book I still live by is Steve Peters’s The Chimp Paradox, which has some similar ideas about quieting the crazed ego-animal within. Ultimately, if you can let Self 2 take control, you can enter the mythic space of the Zone or Flow, which is, according to Daniel Kahneman’s incredible book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the most optimal place a human can reach.

Scarlett Thomas was born in London. She is the author of highly acclaimed contemporary cult novels including The End of Mr. Y, which was longlisted for the Orange Broadband Prize for Fiction; Oligarchy; The Seed Collectors; PopCo; The Sleepwalkers; The Runner; and the Worldquake series of middle grade books. Her novels have sold over half a million copies worldwide and been translated into twenty-six languages. Scarlett is professor of creative writing and contemporary fiction at the University of Kent. Find out more at ScarThomas.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the emotional punch in the gut of Andrey Zvyagintsev’s debut feature, The Return (2003), about an estranged father who takes his two teenage sons on a camping trip, has remained with me, even though I first saw it more than twenty years ago at the Toronto Film Festival. Since then, Zvyagintsev has directed five more films, two of which—Leviathan (2014) and Loveless (2017)—were nominated for Best Foreign Language Film at the Academy Awards. His most recent feature, Minotaur (2026), which is set against the backdrop of mobilization for the war in Ukraine, won the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival.

Based on Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife (1969), Minotaur, for the most part, is an intimate family drama. Successful businessman Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) suspects his wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) of having an affair. Their son, Seryozha, is being bullied at school, and the mayor of the fictional Russian city where the film is set, demands that business owners provide him with a list of employees to be conscripted as soldiers—essentially, cannon fodder.

The story unfolds methodically and slowly in the family’s gorgeous home surrounded by trees, on quiet city streets, and in Galina’s lover’s apartment—until it erupts into violence.

In a recent development, zvyagintsev lives in France and is presently at work on a newly introduced film (that I thought was called Jupiter—more details below) about a Russian oligarch. We spoke on Zoom via a translator. The interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

A heads up: possible spoilers in the discussion.

Industry observers note that radha Vatsal: I want to start with some general observations: that fathers, wealth or power, and violence, often in the form of unexpected deaths, seem to be a theme that crop up frequently in your films. But there’s also a mythical dimension that we’ve seen in some of the titles like Minotaur and Leviathan, and I’m curious what draws you to this mythical element.

In a recent development, andrey Zvyagintsev: Only two out of six films have a mythological reference—Leviathan and Minotaur. Only two.

AZ: Jupiter, no, it’s a working title.

RV: Okay. All right, so then maybe–.

AZ: Jupiter is a name we no longer aim to use because in the Venice Film Festival this year, there was a film named Jupiter. So we could no longer use that name. They did it faster than we could.

According to recent reports, [But to answer your question,] Minotaur, the film, has two sides to it. One is a personal family story, and the other is a story about society. So we could say that there are two films inside Minotaur, and they both have a very strong connection to each other. And they are represented in the title “Minotaur.”.

Well, the first one, as you know from Greek mythology, is the mythological monster that lives in the labyrinth and demands human sacrifices. And then the other part, the more intimate family side—Balzac has a work called “The Physiology of Marriage” [1829] and the subtitle is “Meditations.” The interesting thing is that Balzac was twenty-five when he wrote that work. He was a very, very young man, and it’s really astonishing that someone so young has such an insight into family and married life.

According to recent reports, there is a part where Balzac writes that marital life is like a labyrinth, where the husband wanders in anxiety and watches over his wife. And the husband experiences anxiety when he sees ambiguity, secrets, something unknown in the wife, and he waits anxiously in case there might be a lover around the corner of the labyrinth.

Recent findings suggest that and there is a phrase that Balzac writes, and I’m going to try to quote it to you: That while the husband is wandering around the labyrinth, he’s waiting for the lover to jump out from around the corner; and the lover “minotaurizes”—so making minotaur into a verb—the husband. “Minotaurizes”—that’s the word Balzac uses.

The metaphor is quite simple because for Balzac to give the husband horns, as the minotaur has horns, means to cheat on the husband. But I think it’s also interesting that we do not know what this encounter will entail, and the lover may very well be also the victim of the situation.

So to go back to your question, the title works in two respects and has two sides and explanations to it.

RV: I wanted to discuss the use of interior space in Minotaur. I was very struck by the house. Like the apartment in Elena [Zyvagintsev’s domestic/crime drama from 2011], Gleb and Galina’s home feels like its own character in the film. And there’s a lot of glass and expensive surfaces. It’s also very restrained and tasteful, and it doesn’t match up to the idea we have in the west of fresh money in Russia being very flashy and in your face.

So I was wondering if you could talk about how you center their home, and also your choice of the décor in their home and the restraint.

According to recent reports, AZ: I can tell you that fresh money—especially the Russians, you can obviously find some crazy mansions and different manifestations of wealth. Much more ostentatious. This house is probably worth $2 to $3 million, which is not a lot of money for a really wealthy Russian businessman.

It was incredibly lucky to encounter a house like this in Riga, in Latvia, where we were shooting, because most houses there have this very European kind of look to them, which is not the style of houses you can find in Russia. And so this house was definitely an exception, and we were lucky to find it.

Recent findings suggest that and in the case of Elena, both Elena’s apartment with Vladimir, her husband, and the apartment where her son Seryozha lives with his family—it was all built for the film. In the case of the house you see in Minotaur, this is a house that belongs to the architect who built it, and he actually lives in it. And the only set that was built for Minotaur is the apartment of Anton, the lover. That’s a studio apartment that was built specifically for the film.

RV: The extended sequence of violence that takes place halfway through the film, without any dialogue, is so engrossing. And I was wondering whether that whole sequence was planned or was some of it improvised? It feels like it takes place in real time.

Recent findings suggest that AZ: It was not improvised at all. It was fully planned beat by beat because every scene that involves blood is automatically very hard to do because you have to wash the blood away after every take and then re-spill it. So it takes a lot of time and effort to do that.

So, as I noted, we planned everything well in advance and in a very detailed manner. And we spent five days shooting at the apartment. So day one was love scenes between Galina and her lover. The second day was the encounter between the lover and the husband; and then days three, four, five were all dedicated to the murder scene and the aftermath. So we gave our guy one day to enjoy love, and then the other days, he was getting murdered.

RV: Gleb’s advice to Seryozha when Seryozha tells him that he’s being bullied at school. I expected Glib to be more brutal, and I was surprised that he gave him quite mild advice of how to deal with the bullies.

AZ: You seem to be the only person to think it was mild advice. Where are you from?

RV: India, but I live in New York.

AZ:  Russia is a very patriarchal country, and this is how it happens there. The man is the head of the family. And some 100 years ago, children were not even allowed to start eating before the father starts. And if they did, they could be struck with a wooden spoon on their forehead. So this is regarded by many as a normal form of communication between father and children in Russia.

And, this is an key detail: Gleb starts with saying you have to grab [the bully] by the collar, but then he notes, do not touch him, but just say with the same expression, tell him very deliberately, if you do something like this one more time… So the advice has two parts to it.

I’m not entirely sure what the tool is against bullying at school and the way children sometimes relate to each other in an angry or violent manner. It’s a difficult conversation. So, it’s hard to tell what the right reaction would be.

Sources indicate that this situation is very strange for me. If you have better advice on what to do if a child is getting bullied at school, I would love to hear it because I have a teenage son who is at school in France, in a boarding school, and he also had a problem with bullying, and I also had to give him some advice. My advice was more delicate, but I did explain to him that you have to face the person who tries to bully you and, you know, at least have a conversation.

And going back to your first question about my titles having a mythological connotation, I made a joke earlier about Venice, you know, having a film in competition that was named Jupiter.

It has been revealed that but the truth is, I thought to myself that I probably have a few too many mythological titles. So my fresh film will be called something else, which I cannot tell you right now, but it will be something much better and much more interesting.

RV: Thank you very much. I look forward to seeing it.

In a recent development, radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The Upcoming York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This isn’t another product job.

It’s the chance to define a new category : The Operating System (OS) for Human Greatness Augmented with AI.

Science-backed. Design-led. AI-powered. Global.

A chance to build an AI-native Product Department.

You’ll be working with the most complex data in the world : the human mind.

Deep inside you are looking for a new adventure with….

🚀Ambition around AI field : Smart teammates driven to create an iconic, international product.

🔥Impact : you strive to make a real difference in the company's growth, and not be a number in a big organization.

😍Mission : knowing your greatness left a mark in people's lives, through technology and behavioral science.

At Paradox, we believe that greatness is trainable.

That’s why we want to empower people at scale by leveraging cutting edge technologies like AI, and crafting user experiences with outstanding aesthetics.

- Human Intelligence (coaches, peers, and mentors).

- Structured Intelligence (protocols, mental models, rituals),.

- Technological Intelligence (AI personalization, feedback loops, adaptive journeys).

To create one seamless ecosystem: Paradox OS.

This is why we are looking for a PM to make Paradox a category-defining global brand loved for its product.

This is a full-time position from our beautiful offices in Dubai, Paris or Lisbon or remotely anywhere in the world.

We believe self-help is broken.Most learning platforms are used the same way : consuming generic theories, getting quick highs, ending with no real change.

It has been revealed that at Paradox, we believe people deserve more.More than content. More than motivation.

They deserve a system that knows them, one that adapts, challenges, and grows with them.

We believe that every human learns differently, and that technology can do more than entertain or save time.It can translate insight into transformation, through AI personalization, lean experimentation, and deep psychological understanding.

Because learning shouldn’t just make you feel inspired for a day, it should change how you live, think, and create.

At Paradox, we want to re-invent how people grow.

We do not build another course or coaching app but the Operating System for Greatness.

Founded by David Laroche - a creator followed by over 2 million people and known for his interviews with icons like Tony Parker, Mike Horn, Richard Branson, and Gad Elmaleh, Paradox aims to build something that will live beyond any individual (including its founder), for decades to come.

Our ambition is to compete with players like Mindvalley (150M ARR), but with a sharper vision, grounded protocols for achievers, people who want more for their life, refusing mediocrity.

To do that, we bring together designers, tech, coaches, and filmmakers to create learning experiences that are cinematic, precise, and effective.

It has been revealed that we move fast, aim high, and hold ourselves to the standards of Apple, Spotify, and MasterClass. No fluff, focused on meaningful impact.

While others hide their numbers, we want to let our results speak loudly for us.

Get obsessed with transforming our clients’ lives and let those transformations be our marketing.

We want to build an AI-native company, with agents in every department doing the work alongside our people.

In product, that means building a self-learning AI for product management: a system that learns from every user signal, experiment and release, and gets sharper at deciding what to build next.

For our clients, it means a self-learning AI that serves them through psychology and coaching, and gets better at helping each person change with every interaction.

You won’t just use AI tools: you’ll help design the agents, loops and feedback systems that make Paradox learn faster than anyone else.

-----------------------------------------.

As Product Manager, you’ll be the architect of a new category, transforming growth into a living ecosystem powered by AI, behavioral science, and design.

You won’t just build features, you’ll craft experiences that rewire behavior.

You’re the architect bringing clarity between vision and execution, the person who turns “we should build this” into “it’s live, here’s the data and tangible impact.”.

Every product cycle you lead will integrate:.

Protocols : guided frameworks grounded in psychology that rewire perception, emotion, and action.

Pods : human connection, accountability, and shared rituals.

Loops : adaptive, AI-powered coaching cycles that evolve with each user.

Personalization : experiences that feel uniquely theirs, every time.

Going from a successful personal brand, to an international tech-driven iconic brand, is far from easy. It will be messy, chaotic - requiring constant iterations on MVPs and innovation in tech. Therefore to achieve this here are :.

-----------------------------------------.

Translate the founder’s strategic vision into a clear product strategy.

Build and maintain the roadmap that connects business goals, user outcomes, and technological innovation.

Ensure every feature supports the evolution of the Paradox ecosystem: Loops, PX Agents, Protocols, Membership.

Be obsessed with user problems : talk to users weekly, analyze patterns, and identify where transformation breaks.

Turn insights from behavioral science, coaching psychology, and learning design into actionable product hypotheses.

Design loops, feedback, and rituals that make growth tangible.

build for both the heart (inspiration) and the brain (structure).

Apply Lean Startup methodology and scientific thinking to validate ideas through MVPs, not opinions.

Design experiments and measurable success metrics before building.

Iterate on a weekly basis on upcoming hypothesis.

Define and track product success metrics (activation, retention, transformation rates).

Connect data to business KPIs, know how your product drives lifetime value, not just engagement.

We don’t track metrics just for internal dashboards, we track them also to prove transformation.

Help marketing leverage this data to fuel authentic, evidence-based storytelling — showing the world what real transformation looks like.

Create a visceral experience that translates into emotions of inspiration, awe from owners.

Use a Science-backed, Cinematic, Contrarian style : Every product touchpoint should be grounded in behavioral science, expressed with cinematic beauty, and challenge conventions.

-----------------------------------------.

3–6 years as a Product Manager / Product Owner in EdTech, SaaS, or Consumer Tech.

Bonus: experience in AI-driven products, learning design, or personal development platforms.

You’ve shipped at least one major feature or product end-to-end, and can show measurable results.

Uses Figma comfortably, prototypes directly.

Craft-obsessed : You get things done, you love to work much beyond 9-5, you have a doer mentality, a bias for outcomes and want to be a beast in your field.

User & Impact Obsessed: You think in outcomes, not outputs, you care about transformation.

Analytical & System Thinker: You can turn a vague problem into a clear hypothesis, metrics, and roadmap.

Digital & AI savvy : you’re able to build AI Agents (if not, you demonstrate ability to learn while applying).

Cross-disciplinary Curiosity: You speak both tech and human; You can move from vision to spreadsheet to Figma.

English: Fluent English, you can hold a conversation on specific details with English-speaking colleagues.

Our chosen language for written communication is English.

--------------------------------.

❌ If you need clarity before chaos — wrong place.❌ If you prefer balance over intensity — wrong season.❌ If you build to deliver, not to elevate — wrong mission.

❌Surface-level Vision Alignment : you like the idea of Paradox but doesn’t want to get the depth. Paradox is design-led; you must touch the product, not just manage it.

✅ If you’re obsessed with systems, psychology, and design…✅ If you dream of using AI to amplify what makes us human….

Build a product that fuses neuroscience, design, and AI to reinvent how humans grow.

The chance to build a product that could redefine human potential.

Work with filmmakers, psychologists, engineers, and creatives obsessed with impact.

In the heart of our headquarters stands the 100 000 Dreams Wall,.

Every photo on that wall is a life rewritten:.

“I found peace with my father.”.

You will play a crucial role in the development of an Iconic Product.

-> 🏅Being surrounded by A-players who strive to perform.

But you don’t just want a competitive paycheck, you also want….

-> Playing a crucial role in the development of a company whose content and products will be used by millions of people.

-> Waking up in the morning feeling like you are making a difference is something!We receive messages every day from clients who have successfully lost weight, quit smoking, reached a milestone in their business, built better relationships, and made positive changes in their lives.

-> ❤️ Contributing to the Paradox Foundation (our non-profit), dedicated to empower teenagers.

But that's not all, we believe that driven people deserve….

-> 😎A firm culture based on autonomy & accountability.

-> 🌎A remote culture from day one with the freedom to work from wherever you want.

-> 🏤Magnificent office in Dubai, Paris, Lisbon - it feels like home :).

-> 🧍‍♀️Standing desks paid by the firm if you live far from our offices.

-> 💻Work on Mac, for us it counts :).

-> 🏀350€ per year paid by the tech giant to take care of yourself ( for your gym, or dance class or whatever make you feel great).

-> 📚150€ of books or education - At Paradox, we are learner lovers and we want to support you in that.

-> 🔥6 1:1coachings - A Paradox Coach supporting you on anything personal or professional, we want you to live your best life.

⚠️ To complete the recruitment process, each candidate must organize calls with his or her previous managers. If you are not comfortable with this : do not apply ⚠️.

If all this sounds good to you, come and write the next chapter with us 🚀🚀🚀🚀.

That job description resonated with you?

Here is your tailor made hiring process.

📃 A 6 to 8 minutes application survey (with a short video assignment).

💻 A 30mn video call with Timy, HR, to deep dive into your career path and ambitions.

💻 A 1h video call with Timy, HR, to discuss how you'd fit into Paradox’s Product team.

💻 A 1h culture-fit video call, to assess alignment with our values and mindset.

💻 A 1h final video call with David, CEO, to discuss Product Vision and the next milestones to build.

💼 Reference check to understand how you operate across environments and help set you up for a smooth onboarding.

Sources indicate that our recruitment process is tailored to do our best to avoid that you or us realize that we’re not a perfect fit. Every step serves a purpose and will allow us to get to know you better as much as it’ll help you understand more where you’ll be stepping in.

We also want you to have time to ask all of your questions regarding the mission, the long-term vision of your team and the manufacturer, our values, with the relevant interlocutor in front of you.

If you believe design and AI can awaken what’s best in us then this isn’t a career move.

Let’s build the Operating System for Greatness.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 18, 2026, 10:34 am CST.

According to recent reports, A former Motley Rice attorney was sentenced Monday in Charleston, South Carolina, to 87 months in prison and ordered to pay more than $2.5 million in restitution. (Image from Shutterstock).

A former Motley Rice attorney was sentenced Monday in Charleston, South Carolina, to 87 months in prison and ordered to pay more than $2.5 million in restitution for defrauding the law firm through fictitious companies and ‌false settlement claims.

William Christopher Swett, 42, had previously pleaded guilty to four counts of ​wire fraud and four counts of money laundering, according to a story by Reuters.

A lawyer ​at South Carolina-based ⁠Motley Rice for 12 years, Swett had a severe gambling addiction and substance abuse complications, according to court papers filed on his behalf.

In a recent development, prosecutors have alleged that Swett profited for years ⁠by creating fictitious legal services companies that received reimbursements from Motley Rice. In addition, he allegedly filed fake personal injury claims for family members and put the proceeds into bank accounts that he controlled.

#55630. Beyond Lupin: The Brazen Gentlemen Thieves of Fiction

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1115 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

Beyond Lupin: The Brazen Gentlemen Thieves of Fiction

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Assane Diop has no use for weapons or threats as he plunders Parisian homes and museums.
  • He models his stylish crimes on the escapades of Arsène Lupin, the top-hatted, monocle-wearing creation of French novelist Maurice Leblanc.
  • Diop’s caper-filled quest for justice made the show one of Netflix’s most successful foreign-made franchises by the time it went on hiatus in the fall of 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Assane Diop has no use for weapons or threats as he plunders Parisian homes and museums. His meticulously planned heists are executed with a showman’s flair. The anti-hero of the hit Netflix series Lupin, portrayed to perfection by actor Omar Sy, Diop dons elaborate disguises, slips into fake identities, and turns on the charm as he swipes priceless gems and outwits the police.

He models his stylish crimes on the escapades of Arsène Lupin, the top-hatted, monocle-wearing creation of French novelist Maurice Leblanc. Lupin made his debut in 1905, at the height of the glamorous Belle Époque, and was featured in two dozen novels and short story collections. A skilled burglar and a master of disguise, this impish shapeshifter relishes the challenge of stealing the un-stealable and often returns the treasures he pilfers. He’s more interested in righting wrongs than living off ill-gotten gains. So is Diop – he’s determined to exonerate his father, who was wrongly accused of stealing a priceless necklace from the powerful and corrupt businessman Hubert Pellegrini.

Diop’s caper-filled quest for justice made the show one of Netflix’s most successful foreign-made franchises by the time it went on hiatus in the fall of 2023. As Lupin returns for a long-anticipated fourth season, here’s a lineup of five of the slickest gentlemen thieves of fiction:.

Recent findings suggest that A.J. Raffles: Lupin was France’s answer to a wildly popular English thief of fiction. In 1898, E. W. Hornung (the brother-in-law of Arthur Conan Doyle) published the first of twenty-six stories on the adventures of Arthur Raffles, a London man-about-town and star cricket player who steals to support his expensive lifestyle and keep up appearances. His speciality is cracking safes and he enlists a sidekick from his school days, Bunny Manders, as a partner-in-crime.

It has been revealed that despite his crooked side-gig, Raffles adheres to a gentlemanly moral code. He shudders at the thought of preying on a host or a friend, and rarely packs a gun when he sets out to steal. “It would be very awkward if anything went wrong,” he tells Manders. “One might use it, and that’s not the game at all.” He stalks the corrupt and the obscenely wealthy, reasoning that “the immorally rich” are the logical targets for a “richly immoral” thief like himself.

Hercule Flambeau: His name may sound like that of a certain Belgian detective, but Flambeau’s obsession is stealing jewels, not solving crimes. That changes after a run-in with a priest and part-time detective dreamed up by writer G.K. Chesterton. In the first Father Brown short story, “The Blue Cross,” published in 1910, the clergyman with a kindly demeanor and a keen sense of human nature foils Flambeau’s attempt to steal a religious relic.

Recent findings suggest that like Lupin, Flambeau is one of France’s most-wanted criminals – Chesterton described him as a “colossus of crime” with a long record of “ingenious and wholesale robbery.” And like Lupin, he can disguise himself and hide in plain sight, despite being over six feet tall. He is also “a startling acrobat,” wrote his creator, who “could leap like a grasshopper and melt into the tree-tops like a monkey.” Flambeau became a recurring character, appearing in more than a dozen of the fifty-three Father Brown stories, and not only reforms but eventually helps the clergyman to crack cases.

According to recent reports, john Robie: It’s the early 1950s on the French Riviera and Robie, a wily burglar whose agility earned him the nickname “Le Chat” before he was caught and imprisoned, is forced out of retirement when a copycat makes him a suspect in new crimes. The protagonist in American travel writer David Dodge’s 1952 novel To Catch a Thief sets out to trap his doppelgänger.

In a recent development, robie is the consummate gentleman thief – dashing, clever, a master of his calling. Who better to portray him when Alfred Hitchcock brought the story to the big screen in 1955 than the king of suave, Cary Grant. “For what it’s worth,” Grant-as-Robie points out in a line added for the movie, “I never stole from anybody who would go hungry.”.

Industry observers note that sir Charles Lytton: Peter Sellers’s hilariously inept Inspector Jacques Clouseau debuted in the 1963 movie The Pink Panther, but the real star of the blockbuster franchise’s first instalment was David Niven. He was cast as the debonaire playboy Sir Charles Lytton, who leads a double life as an elusive jewel thief known as “The Phantom.” Niven was an inspired choice – he played Raffles on screen in 1939, in one of many films to feature Hornung’s character.

The Pink Panther is reputed to be the world’s largest diamond and Lytton has come to a ski resort in the Italian Alps to steal it. The bumbling Clouseau is there to try to stop him. Niven may have enjoyed top billing as a classy crook but Sellers’s over-the-top performance stole the show and hijacked the franchise.

Danny Ocean: Frank Sinatra was the first to tackle the role of the ringleader of a gang of thieves who rob five Las Vegas casinos on Upcoming Year’s Eve in the 1960 movie Ocean’s 11. George Clooney revived the character four decades later in 2001’s Ocean’s Eleven, with Danny assembling a team of skilled crooks (an all-star cast that includes Brad Pitt and Matt Damon) to loot a supposedly impregnable Vegas vault.

In a recent development, the movie inspired two sequels, with the gang reuniting to steal a Fabergé egg in Ocean’s Twelve and a casino’s cash and a trove of diamonds in Ocean’s Thirteen. In each movie the targets are fellow thieves or ruthless, unscrupulous moguls. The heists are filled with Lupin-worthy disguises and deceptions and Clooney is a natural for the modern iteration of the cool, classy crook.

Recent findings suggest that it’s little wonder the gentleman thief is a staple of fiction. His victims are fellow travellers who deserve to be cut down to size, or have insurance policies or pockets deep enough to absorb their losses. Admiring their audacity and cheering them on is a guilty pleasure we can all enjoy.

According to recent reports, dean Jobb’s latest true crime book, A Gentleman and a Thief: The Daring Jewel Heists of a Jazz Age Rogue (Algonquin Books and HarperCollins Canada), is a Fresh York Times Editors’ Choice and a national bestseller in Canada. It’s the story of Arthur Barry, who charmed the elite of 1920s New York City while planning and executing some of the most brazen jewel thefts in history. Find him at deanjobb.com.

#55628. The top five Watsons (read: “often impressed best friend narrators”) in crime fiction

The top five Watsons (read: “often impressed best friend narrators”) in crime fiction

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I don’t mean this literally, I mean this professionally.
  • Industry observers note that that’s what Watson DOES in the Sherlock Holmes series.
  • Assembled for your reading pleasure are five series that follow this general formula: brilliant detective, awed chronicler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every great detective needs a Watson.

Industry observers note that I don’t mean this literally, I mean this professionally. By “Watson,” I refer to the archetype of the Very Impressed Best Friend And Narrator. A hype man who also tells the story. A deputy who keeps going “wow, look at this guy” as he tells you about this guy. Bonus points if he’s also this guy’s roommate.

Industry observers note that that’s what Watson DOES in the Sherlock Holmes series. He’s a carnival barker and a nonfiction writer. Sherlock Holmes is not only his friend, he’s his subject. Watson isn’t only HIS best friend, he’s his audience. But he’s also his publicist. He‘s fascinated by Holmes, and he knows tons of people will also be fascinated by Holmes. His job is PR, and man does he do it well.

Assembled for your reading pleasure are five series that follow this general formula: brilliant detective, awed chronicler.

Watson: Archie Goodwin  Detective: Nero Wolfe.

Industry observers note that in the beloved Rex Stout series, the young Archie Goodwin narrates AND does all the legwork for the affluent, grouchy, high-on-the-horse bibliophile and private detective Nero Wolfe who hates leaving his luxurious brownstone. Archie, a handsome and dapper young man, is a quick-witted, fast-talking factotum. And he’s always pretty impressed with the mental calculations of his sedentary boss.

Watson: S.S. Van Dine Detective: Philo Vance.

S.S. Van Dine takes the Watson gambit even further than Watson does. He is a real person, the real-life writer of the Philo Vance books (though “S.S. Van Dine was a pen name; his real name was Willard Huntington Wright), who writes himself into the stories as the best friend of the brilliant, suave, dandyish detective Philo Vance. Here, he’s not Vance’s creator, merely his chronicler, and the two solve innumerable mysteries together during the Jazz Age.

Sources indicate that watson: Unnamed  Detective: C. Auguste Dupin.

It has been revealed that we don’t know the name of the guy who narrates his friend and roommate Auguste Dupin’s feats of investigation, but he is really the OG Watson. They meet at various rare booksellers and eventually hit it off, becoming pals and then deciding to move in together.

Watson: Capt. Arthur Hastings  Detective: Hercule Poirot.

Hercule Poirot’s best friend Arthur Hastings doesn’t narrate ALL the Poirot stories (he narrates eight of thirty-three novels, and twenty-one of fifty-one short stories), because, after Hastings meets a beautiful music hall performer half his age in Murder on the Links, he marries her and eventually moves with her to South America, where they have four kids. But Hastings appears sprinkled throughout the Poirot canon, because he returns to England for business a lot. So they get together and crime-solve then.

Watson: Anthony Horowitz Detective: Daniel Hawthorne.

According to recent reports, look, I’d have such a soft spot for Anthony Horowitz even WITHOUT the these books, simply because I grew up reading the Alex Rider series. But the Horowitz and Hawthorne mysteries, in which “Horowitz himself” tags along as the sidekick and narrator (he’s NOT ONLY the Watson, here, but Van Dine). Their work is very collaborative (and these books are sneaky, since Hawthorne isn’t the real mastermind, but Horowitz himself).

According to recent reports, olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 18, 2026, 11:34 am CST.

    In a recent development, david Beckham poses after he was made a knight bachelor at an investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle on Nov. 4, 2025, in Windsor, England. (Photo by Andrew Matthews/Getty Images).

    A German beauty group that makes and distributes former soccer player David Beckham’s fragrance line has kicked out at the soccer icon’s lawsuit against them, asking a Fresh York court to dismiss the case.

    The Associated Press reported Tuesday that German-based Coty has argued that the New York Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction, and that Beckham’s commercial entity DB Ventures is simply using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from their deal to sign with another firm.

    DB Ventures had originally filed suit in April, alleging that Beckham’s brand of luxury colognes and fragrances were being sold at gas stations and discount stores in violation of their agreement.

    According to the AP, Beckham’s name is a famous global brand synonymous with luxury and elegance.

    “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the complaint said. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”.

    According to the AP, DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.

    Coty told the AP that it strongly disputes the claims and would not comment further on ongoing litigation. Authentic Brands, DB Ventures’ parent company, declined to comment to the AP.

    Beckham, a former Manchester United, Real Madrid, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain and LA Galaxy player who captained the English national football team and was knighted in 2025, has built a business career that includes co-owning soccer team Inter Miami.

    According to the Sunday Times, he is the first billionaire sports figure in the United Kingdom, having a combined net worth of about $1.58 billion with his wife, Victoria Beckham, a former member of the Spice Girls music group.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 18, 2026, 12:42 pm CST.

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the state’s threshold for intoxication. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.

    It has been revealed that warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M. Chmura, 63, was found guilty of intoxication while driving his Ford Fusion into a parked bus that was displaying hazard lights March 25. But the court rejected the charge of Chmura driving with an elevated high blood alcohol content of 0.17 or greater, according to coverage on Law360.

    Novi 52nd District Court Judge David Law noted that Chmura’s judgment had been affected, but he questioned the blood alcohol concentration at the time of the crash.

    Sources indicate that “This court may think it knows the answer to whether or not this was a high BAC case,” Law noted. “But thinking it knows is not enough. It needs to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.”.

    Recent findings suggest that A bus driver sitting inside the bus waiting to resume his route was uninjured in the crash. Sterling Heights, Michigan, police officer Jonathan Journeau testified that Chmura smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech and couldn’t maintain his balance.

    In a recent development, chmura’s attorney, David J. Kramer of the David J. Kramer Law Firm, argued that prosecutors could not establish the higher offense because Journeau failed to determine when the judge’s final alcoholic beverage was consumed.

    Justice Department Announces Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.
    • “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M.
    • In a recent development, “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

    “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement shows that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”.

    In a recent development, “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division rapidly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure demonstrates that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”.

    Industry observers note that “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”.

    Sources indicate that “The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”.

    “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” remarked Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”.

    Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California.

    In a recent development, today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California revealed the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

    North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

    It has been revealed that during the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the newly introduced victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

    Sources indicate that the North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

    The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

    The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

    The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance.

    Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

    Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

    The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

    #55613. Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1282 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that by Scott A.
    • According to recent reports, for two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer.
    • Recent findings suggest that systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that by Scott A. Meyers and Michael Adler.

    According to recent reports, for two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer. That is no longer enough.

    Recent findings suggest that systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps. Used well, they can reduce routine work, freeing lawyers for judgment and client advice.

    In a recent development, the profession built its supervision framework around people and bounded tools. An agentic system fits neither model: It has no license to lose or judgment to train, yet acts across a workflow with autonomy the Model Rules do not squarely address.

    When AI moves from answering questions to executing multistep legal workflows, what does meaningful human oversight look like?

    The unit of supervision is no longer an answer; it is a system of delegated decisions.

    In a recent development, the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct anticipated part of this shift. In 2012, the ABA changed Rule 5.3’s title from “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistants” to “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance.” Its comments encompassed technology-enabled services; a companion resolution added technological competence to what became Comment 8 of Rule 1.1. In 2024, Formal Opinion 512 applied Rules 1.1, 5.1, and 5.3 to lawyers’ use of generative AI and their supervision of the people and providers using it.

    Industry observers note that that guidance remains organized around a tool: review its output, protect client information, train users and assess providers. It offers less direction when the system executes the workflow, deciding which documents to pull, which facts matter, and what goes where—decisions the finished product may not reveal. Reviewing only the output confirms the car arrived, not its route. Supervision of output is not supervision of process.

    Recent findings suggest that METR’s May 2026 report sharpens the point. Assessing agents inside frontier developers (or entities that train AI models), it found them exceeding intended bounds and misleading customers about their work, especially on difficult tasks. It did not study law firm deployments, and routine monitoring might have caught every incident because an independent record existed. The lesson: A lawyer cannot treat an agent’s account as the record of its work. That account is another output of the same probabilistic process, which has training incentives that can reward telling users what they want to hear. Asking the agent to double-check itself is not an independent control.

    Sources indicate that accountability cannot rest solely with whoever pressed “run.” It must be institutional and individual, extending to those who designed, approved and maintained the workflow. Every deployed workflow should have a named lawyer-owner authorized to pause it, just as every matter has a responsible partner. This does not displace the matter lawyer’s responsibilities. The owner’s authority must permit suspension on suspicion alone before a committee convenes or a vendor responds. Ownership without it is a label.

    In a recent development, final output review remains necessary. Oversight must also cover consequential junctures: privilege calls, external communications, filings and anything irreversible or beyond client authorization. Supervision begins at design time: deciding what a workflow may do independently, its latitude to reason, and where it must stop and ask. Every firm should be able to answer: Where can this system act without a human seeing it first, and who decided that?

    In a recent development, A tested record on comparable work can justify less intensive routine checking, though never at those consequential junctures. Greater autonomy should be approved and recorded. Material changes to the model, tools, permissions or workflow should trigger reassessment and renewed authorization.

    Autonomy bundles three permissions requiring separate calibration: generating work product, accessing sensitive information, and acting in firm or client systems. Permissions should narrow as consequences grow: broad room to draft; matter-scoped room to read; and narrow, logged room to act. A first-year may draft the memo; nobody gives them unilateral wire authority. The grant of action is never implied by the grant of access.

    Industry observers note that if a firm cannot trace what a system did, it cannot supervise it; where reasoning cannot be audited, behavior must be. Otherwise, recordkeeping, preservation, and verification of representations to clients, courts, and third parties may suffer. Three mechanisms matter: an audit trail independent of the agent’s reporting, means to interrupt workflows mid-run, and a path to unwind reversible actions—with honesty about those that cannot be reversed. Record model versions and configurations too: Providers upgrade continuously, and a workflow validated in March may differ from August’s.

    Sources indicate that five workflows can be governed individually; 500 cannot. Solo and small practices may use a simple inventory but still need a way to stop a workflow. At scale, governance becomes operational infrastructure: an inventory of deployed systems, risk classification, approval gates, monitoring and reassessment. The profession knows this playbook: Ask a managing partner how conflicts are governed, and you will hear about a system, not a policy.

    Delay accumulates governance debt: workflows deployed faster than they can be inventoried, permissions granted faster than they can be reviewed. Like all debt, it compounds quietly. When data-protection regimes preceded settled enforcement guidance, prudent organizations built from regulatory intent rather than waiting for caselaw. Agentic AI presents the same problem: established duties but no settled operating model.

    Ownership, calibrated oversight, permission limits, traceability, reversibility and governance at scale matter wherever organizations deploy agentic AI. What distinguishes law is that our supervisory duties are explicit and long-standing. We are not a special case. We are an early test case.

    Fortunately, the test is familiar. Lawyers have been supervising work they did not personally perform since the first associate billed their first hour. The question is no longer only whether lawyers can use AI competently. It is whether we can supervise systems that increasingly do the work of the supervised.

    In a recent development, scott A. Meyers is the chairman and CEO, and Michael Adler is the director of artificial intelligence governance and data protection at Akerman, an Am Law 100 law firm.

    #55601. The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1750 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.
    • This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known.
    • Industry observers note that first, a review of the basics.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

    This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

    Industry observers note that first, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

    Industry observers note that this process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal issue in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

    Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

    In a recent development, as noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

    In a recent development, nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an important concern of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

    This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an issue that has been turned down one or more times.

    Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

    The answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

    According to recent reports, but much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 says the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an notable issue of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

    Sources indicate that just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

    The cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

    It has been revealed that and the justices rarely discuss it. In his new book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

    Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

    Many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

    According to recent reports, the clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

    In a recent development, caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

    Sources indicate that question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

    According to recent reports, the number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

    Oddly, no one seems to know why.

    Recent findings suggest that there are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

    Recent findings suggest that these interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

    Different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer latest laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

    It is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a manufacturer based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the issue (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

    Question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

    The Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal problems, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

    Sources indicate that A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

    Industry observers note that the process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

    Steve Wermiel is a professor of practice at American University Washington College of Law, where he has taught a seminar on the Supreme Court for nearly three decades.
